title: Rigoletto
facts: Rigoletto had a triumphant premiere at La Fenice in Venice on 11 March 1851, after serious trouble with the Austrian censors.
The source, Victor Hugo’s play Le roi s’amuse, had been banned in France after its premiere and wasn’t staged again until 1882.
Verdi told Piave to get permission at any cost: “Use four legs, run through the town and find me an influential person.”
Verdi on his hunchbacked jester: “There is a character that is one of the greatest creations that the theatre can boast of.”
The censor flatly refused “La Maledizione” (the working title). One rewrite turned the king into a duke and dropped both the hunchback and the curse; Verdi refused it.
The jester was originally called Triboulet. The name Rigoletto came from a parody comedy, “Rigoletti, or The last of the jesters”.

At the premiere, Felice Varesi (Rigoletto) froze in panic. Verdi pushed him onstage, and he tumbled on clumsily; the audience thought it was a planned gag.
La donna è mobile|La donna e mobile
Verdi kept “La donna è mobile” secret until a few hours before the premiere and forbade anyone to sing or whistle it outside the theatre.
La donna è mobile|La donna e mobile
The morning after the premiere, “La donna è mobile” was being sung in the streets.
Because of censorship, Rigoletto sometimes played in Italy under other names, such as Viscardello, Lionello and Clara de Perth.
“Zitti, zitti” (“Softly, softly”): blindfolded and tricked, Rigoletto holds the ladder while the courtiers abduct his own daughter.
The courtiers gleefully tell the Duke they have captured “Rigoletto’s mistress”. It is really Gilda, his daughter.
Verdi finished the score on 5 February 1851, little more than a month before the premiere.
